title: Data from Information Repositories: Customer Relationship Management Software
shortTitle: Data from Information Repositories: Customer Relationship...
summary: Customer relationship management software is the system of record for customer interactions, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour directed at the data a business holds about the people it serves. Records typically include names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, purchase history, support conversations and sometimes partial payment details, and the platform usually offers reporting, export and integration features that move data in bulk. An adversary with a valid account, an integration key or an interface token can query records directly, often without touching a user interface at all, and can filter down to the subset that interests them. Detection therefore combines application audit logs with data volume analysis: unusually large queries or exports, reports run outside business hours, newly connected applications or integration keys, changes to field level permissions, and access from an address that does not match the account's normal pattern. The distinguishing factor is purpose, which shows up as volume, breadth and destination rather than in any single request.

beginner.definition: Customer relationship management, or CRM, software is a tool that stores everything a company knows about its customers. Salesforce and Microsoft Dynamics are examples. This sub-technique means an attacker mines that customer data. It is the parent idea, aimed at customer records instead of documents.
beginner.whyItMatters: Customer data is valuable and personal at the same time. Attackers can sell it, or use it to trick the customers themselves. Stolen names, emails and phone numbers make fake messages and phone calls far more convincing. Companies may also face fines and lose trust. One integration key can expose millions of records, so access must be watched closely.
howItWorks: The parent technique covers shared repositories; this one targets customer relationship systems.
The attacker signs in with a valid user account, or steals an integration key.
They use search, saved reports or a direct interface to pull matching records.
They narrow the data to what sells best, such as names, emails and phone numbers.
They export in bulk, or send the records to a system outside the company.
They may add their own application key so access continues after a reset.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where the front desk keeps a book of guest names, phone numbers and room preferences. Staff use the book every day to give good service. A temporary worker copies the last five years of pages during a quiet night shift. Weeks later, guests receive calls that mention their exact holiday dates. The book was needed for the job, so nobody had ever questioned who could read it.
takeaways: Customer records are a direct path to fraud and to very convincing phishing.
Integration keys and reporting tools move data in bulk, so watch them closely.
Large exports and odd working hours are stronger clues than a single record view.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent repository technique.
List the kinds of personal data commonly held in customer relationship systems.
Describe how integration keys and reporting features enable bulk data collection.
Identify audit and volume signals that indicate data mining inside such a system.
Explain how stolen customer data supports later phishing campaigns.
